MINERS MEETING AT ST. HELENS. 1 • meeting of miners was held, on Tuesday evening, in the Old Mill, to consider the principle of organisation in re- !crew. to the agitation which is DOM going on. There not so many present as was expected. Mr. Pickett occupied the chair, and in the course of his remarks said that he n4r at the committee the day preview, helping to form the rules, and though there were a few little things which they could not get over he hoped everything would be settled favour- ably to each and every one. With re te once to organisation he thought it meant order and arrangement. If men were down in the dust it was said put them still lower, but he said if a man were going tiown, keep him from falling, and if he were up lift hfin higher. In 188 P they were in • far isetter state of organisation than they were at the present time, and they had a cer- tain amount of money In St. Helena Hardoek, and Wigan which they had oot at preeent owing to lack of organisation. If they had been united as they ought to nave been the reenit. would have been that no unreasonable reductions would have taken place. He did net want to take advantage of the masters, and he did not want the masters to take ad- vantage of their men, but this the masters had done. They mug, however, unite together to protect themselvesand work together whatever their religious or pulltical opinions might 100 Every one of them woe a branch of that great tree on which all classes detemded. It was their duty lobe up and doing and prevent further encroachments upon their rights and privilegee, and avoid 21 a ton being taken off their wages without any notice beinggiven them. lie urged upon them to be unit d to that they might get that which was right, legal, and lawful. lie had told his master that day that hewould not submit to anything unlawful if he knew it. It was hie duty as a servant to I.k well after his master's pnmerty, and it was the master's duty ae toaster to eon he wee paid for hie work. Ile aleo told his master that he was working too many hour., and the coal they were getting was greater than the demand, and they mug regulate the markets. If the master was not getting enfficient for hia coal he mug raise the price, iso that the public might pay for it. Mr. Leans, of Wigan, then addreassl the meeting, and said that employers of labour believed in organisation, and would meet together and discuss questions affecting their trade, but they ought to give that freedom to working men. Where woe the employer who could not justify hitneelf in belonging to an emaciation to rule and regulate and discuss thing, for hie own interest, both in advancing and reducing their men's wages ? If that employer did not give his employee the privilege of having a say in the mat- ter, then he had no sytnpathy or Christianity in him. At Durham nothing was done by the emagwyere without con- sulting their men and discuesing the question in • friendly way. But were they treated so in West Lancashire P No. The reason was because they could not cmnmand attention on account of Moir want of organisation. The truck system had been abolished by the organisation of the men, and in 1889, in Staffordshire, when the men were working from 10 to 12 hours • day, and the men were paid fortnightly or monthly, he, with othere, went to lift hie voice against it, and uried toe necessity of orgtnieation,andina short time the net combined, and they were paid weekly. After pointing out several other henefits which had been derived from thorough organisation. The speaker referred to the weigh- ing clause, and said that Mr. Cross, the Home Secretary, had remarked that he was sorry they did not take advantage of the privilege which was given them as the Act of Parlia- ment said that the men Is a pit could appoint two or three men to go down the pit and make • report of what they saw going oa. But that could not be well carritsl out without organisation. There was, however, good newt. There was a spirit of unity all through Lancashire, and in Bolton where oronisation was almost complete. More than 4,000 miners had joined the society during the last three weeks. (Cheers.) He concluded by urging them to esMblish a district. Every rule would go berme the lodges to be kevestigated and criti- cised, and would he open to criticism. At the suggestion of the CHAIRMAN, the entire audience almost held up their hands as a proof of their belief In organisation , and we understand that on Monday a district lodge wit be formed.

The Clerk was ordered to acknow- ledge the letter and to make application for sanction of £lO 3s. 3d. paid during the year for teacher.' returns pre- vious to the audit. At a meeting, held oa the 19th January, the School Attendance 011icer read his report, and gave for the year ending December, 1879.—N0. On books, 1.982 overage attendances. LAM: absentees. 458. Number on books in September. 1879. 2,110. average attendance, 1,581 . abeentees, 549. The decreased number was attributed to removals by parents seeking employment and the severity of the weather.—instructions were given to the Attendance Officer in some irregular cane to enforce better attendance, especially George Day's children, who were known to be frequently Legging at houses. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 14, 18SO.
THE WIDNES MURDER.

Another set in the Widnee tragedy was played out yesterday afternoon in the Assize Court, at Liver- pool, when Hugh Burns, thirty years of age, Patrick Kean., twenty-one year. of age, and Mary An Tracey, twenty-eight years of age, were declared guilty of having murdered Patrick Tracey, the hus•• band of the last-named prisoner, on the 24th of Oc- tober last, and were sentenced by Lord Chief Jennie. Coleridge to death. A more dastardly, eold-blooded outrage it would be difficult to find in the anna/a of crime, and the terms in which the Lodge addressed the culprite when pawing upon them the dread nen. toner of the law was not one whit too severe. The whole story of the diabolical murder, together with the conclusive evidence upon which the jury convicted Buena, Kearns, and the wife of the murdered man as the perpetrators of the tragedy will be found detailed in another part of this day's Erenich,r. Widnee has for some time enjoyed the unenviable reputation of being the scene of deteetable aets of violence ; and it must be satisfactory to peaceable inhabitants to know that this last tragedy loot to be added to the list of undiscovered crimes in thin loe.ality.

div.head: LIBERAL PARTY AND HOME RULE.
div.p: THE LIBERAL PARTY AND HOME RULE.

The existing relations between the Liberal party and the Home Ru.era is at the preeent time anything but satisfactory, and if before the next general elec- tion there is not a change in the situation, the result can warve fail to be disastroua to the Liberal cause • Whatever may be the opinions entertained by the leading Libendr ;,0 Home Rule, or on the denirability of supporting a mutton for a Parliamentary inquiry :DU' the (elation, they certainly do not approve of the menus the HOme Rule party ad.,pt to obtain their ends. The unwiedom of the Home Rule tartlet', beth in and out of Parliament, is becoming manifest to everybody. Their demand for . inquiry into the question of local legislation for Ireland, and into the existing ceases of Irish discontent and distress is a fair and re.onable one, and one against which it would ill become the Liberal party to raioo the cry of won posoonto. But Laie the leee unwise is it for the Home Ruler. in the various large town, throughout Great Britain where they haves large vote, to make this a test question, and to ask candidates to pledge themselves to vote forir'o'i.ln Liverpool they gained no real advantage by extracting a pledge hem the Liberal candidate to vote for an inquiry, and Lord gainsay was quite aim good a repr.entative of the Home Rule portion of the electors, and quite as able and willing to assist in the passing of me..ee of liberal legislation for Ireland, before as after he made his promise to vote for inquiry. Oa the other hand, by extracting a definite promise front Lord Ramsay, it is certain that the Home Rulen deprived him of the support of a number of Liberals who look upon Home Rule demands with great disfavour, and, perhaps, of a sufficient number to have won him the election. The consequence of this is that Liver- pool Home Rulere have wut to the Imperial Parliament as their representative . out and out supporter of the party that not only refuses them redress, but denounoet those who aupp.t their demands as persons who are guilty of treason to the Sovereign. The lessen is ens that the Liberal party cad Home Rulers alike ought to take to heart. The Home Rulo leaders in Liver- pool and elsewhere must know full well that the party that has done the most for the redress of Irish grievances in the past, and that is still willing to do full justice, even to the extent of reparation for peat wrongs, is the great Liberal party alone. And in view of the coining election not Home Rulers alone, but ail sections of the Liberal party who have their peculiar views on particular subjects, ought to recognise the difficulties that Liberalism has to contend againat to-day, with •united and compact Tory phalanx in their front. The Home Rulers ought to revoirnioe that the spirit of modern Liberalism towarch; Ireland is one of I great friendliness, and, as Lord Ramsay intimated ha I the course of his electioneering speeches at Liverpool last week, that there is every desire not only to do complete justice in the present and to give to Ireland as far as pomade all the advmtages that England pomeases, but to make reparation for past wrong.. I prom the Liberal party Ireland has evelything to hope ,lidestete.,htlime• diseeck-vay,,ivracecedge Asa .nacrpcor election place it beyond a doubt that it will be most unwise for the Home Riders to seek to obtain from Liberal candidates such a definite promise as Lord Ramaay gave, and equally unwise for Liberal candi• dates to so pledge themselves. No better plan could be devised for creating a serious division r in the Liberal piety, and to playing into the hand. j of the Toffee, who are the uncompromising opponents not only of any inquiry into the cease of Ireland's ! condition but--becauae of their great tenderness far the eights and privileges of the landocracy—the oppo- ; nenta also of any honest legialative attempt to ime prove the condition of the Irish tenants. The one striking difference between the Tory and the Liberal view of the Irish difficalty is that while on the one side there is an obstinate determination to look at it and examine it from no other than the landlords point of new. on the otlaer there ie a disposition to- wards a full and impartial inquiry with a view to the passing of remedial meaanres irr.pective of all class prejudices. Amongst other advantages that would result from a large Liberal majority in the new Parlia- ment would undonbtedly be a thoronglily disinter- ' toted attempt to settle the whole Irish question in a . way that would find favour with the great body of the people and happily pat an end once and for ever to Irish grievant.e and diacontent. It is to be hoped, tberef ore, that before the next general election the Irish voters will everywhere recognise the im- portance of extending to the Liberal candidates a generous support without seeking to hamper them with pledges, that are in no way calculated to advance I the cease they profeee to have at heart. In the debate on Mr. Shaw's; amendment on the address, and which was defeated on Tuesday nigh, by 216 votes against It, there wee nothing more re- markable than the sympathetic tone in which several English members addiessed thenmelvea to the sub- ject of Ireland's wrongs and difficulties. Mr. Chamberlain opened fire on the Government in an argumentative speech, in whir-', he maintained that they were deserving of censure for allowing the distress to assume such large proportions as it now does. Hs declared it to be lais opinion that tho Government were in no way alive to the gravity of the position of affairs, and even went the length I of voting for the amendment "in order to ..laow his practiced sympathy with the Irob people who were suffering from a land system which had been found unsatisfactory in every civilised country in the world, and whioh bad been re- formed in every other cnuutry except oar own." Mr. Peter Rylands also supported the amendment, and said that he was oonsiiantiouely in favour of a committee of inquiry into the question of Home Rule, because if it could be shown that there were any better means of govern- tag Ireland than we had at present "the Government and people of chid country ought to know them." Mr. Jacob Bright followed in a similar strain. It is true that these are sot the views of the Marquis of Hart- ington and other lending members of the Oppoeition, htit there is nothing in them inconsistent with
A ROAD!
ROAD,

position whi, b Lord Itartington assumes with regard to Ireland, or with the course he would be prepared to follow if he were in office to-morrow. English Liberal members are by no meant likely to be converted to Iron. Rule, but they recornioo the fact that Ireland has still more grisvancoo to be redeemed. This is Co. and the statesman who can succeed in bringing prosrerity and pea,o to a land where now there is discontent and distr.., would leave behind him a memory to be honoured for above that of the most successful 0 gunpowder and glory" minister that Engboad has ever produced.

The proposal to raise a fulled M Runcorn for the purpose of assisting the sufferers from the Irish Famine, meets Willi) hardly my support. T see dial at the public meeting, called by Mr. Lyon for the consideration or the proposal, reference was tnaile to the fact that the Rev. Father Fennelly, the Roman Catholic priest, did not even put in an appearance There may have been a good cause for the übeence of the reverend gentleman, but surely he might have taken the trouble to pen the Chairman a line expresing his satisfac- tion that such a movement had been startoil, and his regret that he was not able to attend. A gathering of the nature described, without the presence of the reverend father, was film the play of "Hamlet " with Hamlet left out.

Your readers are aware that the overseers of Runcorn have for some time past been in communication with the Local Government Board, for the purpose of obtaining the neces- sary sanction to provide a proper room horohieh to hold vestry nacetings. It was suggested that the meetings should be held in one of the rooms at the Public 11311, but I under- Rand that before the Local Government Board would grant their eanction to such 0 proposal they insisted upon having a lease from the Public Hall Company, who have declined to grant it. The public will probably have to wait several months more before a decision is arrived at in what at first eight would appear a very Guild° matter. Ihe Public Hall at Runcorn is a credit to the town, and I am glad to hear that the members of the company have just received a good dividend, considering these dull times. The Widnes Atlas Chemical Company, which is a limited concern, have just held their yearly meeting and declared a dividend of 12s. per ahem. Not bad, in times when no many companies are either in liquidation or restricting the ephere of their operations. Special eervices are being held by the Runcorn IVesleyan Methodists. The preaching at St. Paul's of late has been very fruitful of spiritual results.

The proposal nmde at the late meeting of the Runcorn I Young Men's Christian Association to increase the charger for membership does not appear to have been received with unmixed satisfaction. These are hardly times in which to miss subscriptions, notwithstanding the wonderful improver scent in chemicals spoken of by the Premier. It is much to be regretted that an msociation which possesses such attractive r.rns and so good a library should have to fall back upec, the kindness of its President (Mr. Robert Shaw) to often.

The amount raised in Runcorn towards the Rowland Hill Memorial Fund is remarkably small—hardly worth men- tioning. It is, however, larger than the sum contributed at Widnes, where, on the Local Honed meeting on Tuesday, the Claairinan reported clod "nothing" had been paid into the bank. on account of the fur..,.

The formation of the Runcorn Debating Society appears to have been a good "hit." The honourable members have, thus far, manifested considerable speaking ability, and the walls of the Bethesda Congregational Schoolroom echo weekly to harangue., some of which are simply terrible, 111 their charges against Her Majesty's Government. Leave has already been granted to the Member for the University of Oxford to bring in a Bill for the amendment of the representation of the people. I hope that peace will be within the walls of the Runcorn St. Stephens, and that the members will take everything mid in good part, and keep clear of personal bickering. tam glad to see that the Widnes Parish Church has been taken in hand by the new Vicar and the Churchwardens, and is likely to be beautified. 'the idea of so altering the entrance to the edifice that the vapours from Messrs. Hutchinson's extensive works cannot enter the building, is a capital one.

A serious charge was brought against the conductors of the Widnes Roman Catholic ball, at a late petty sessiOne at that town, by Mr. Brindle, the superintendent of police; and if that gentleman's statement he correct—and I have no reason to know that it is not—the proceedings at the ball held a year ago were most disgraceful, and such an should cause all true Catholica to blush at the fact of having t heir names connected with it. The Runcorn Cooperative and Provident Society appears to be in a flourishing condition, and they have just declared a dividend at the rate of half-a-crown in the pound. Mr. Fiupatrick, of Wattles, who at one of the annual meetings a year ago created quite a scene by demanding various ex- planations from the directors, has been disposed of in the same manner in which a troublesome member of the House Of Commons is often dealt with—by being appointed to an office. The position given to Mr. Fitzpatrick is that of auditor, and I regret fence that he I S so soon tired of his "blushing banners," for at the half-yearly meeting he an- nounced that he intended to resign. He has evidently found the berth of auditor no had of roses, and he is determined to be rid of it. It is, however, satisfactory to learn that the resell of Mr. Fitzpatrick's investigations into the affairs of the Society have led him to the conviction that they are on • sound financial basis.

Many of these who belong to the timid class of society will be very pleased to bear that a proposal is on foot for placing a policeman on Runcorn foot bridge. The desira- bility of carrying out such a suggestion will not be ques- tioned by those who have to pass the bridge frequently at night. It is a wonder to many people that so few people I complain of being mmu:ted. or stopped upon the bridge. I bappen to know that there are occasionally such CaSe, and it is very rce.aary that ladies should have some protecti.m afforded them, or there may time come when the neg.. lent may be deeply regretted. The indifferent lighting of the structure certainly offers a temptation to roughs ta molest people when the night Itappms to be dark, and if any pl:m he carried out by which this danger cm be avoided, it will be Immo apprciated. Many of your Runcorn readers will he glad to know that some effort ii?., be made to investigate OW alleged nuisance from Messrs. EAT and Chester's chemical works, which has been complained of so often. / am somewhat surprised that such a lover of science as

Mr. G. S. Haalehurst has pored himself to be, should take up the ground that if the footbridge connect,' with the Runcorn railway bridge over the Mersey is widened so at to make it available as a carriage way, a number of serious carriage accidents would inevitably take place. Surely the engineers of the present day could devise some means whereby horses could not see the pmsing trains. The proposed bridge would boot the greatest advantage to Runcorn and Widnes, and I regret to see that Mr. Haslehurst does not stern to belong to the party of progress.

The annual meeting was held on Monday evening, in the same place of worship, Mr. Robert Shaw presiding. The Chair- man referred to the importance of the work in which they were engaged, and to the great necessity which existed for Ii in that immediate neighbourhood. The Rey. C. Bingant (superintendent , read the report of the parent nociety, which showed that 108 missionaries were engaged, and 881 circuits benefited by it. He regretted to say that there was a debt upon the society of £7,500. The Rees. Brown (of London) and Kent (of Farnworth) attended as a deputation, and addressed the tneeting an home ntission work. A rote of thanks was passed to the deputation, on the motion of Mr. S. Robinson. seconded by Mr. Swale. A similar compliment was passed to the chairman, after which the proceedings terminated.

The directors in their report gated that the gross profits of the company for the year, including transfer fees, amounted to £43,951 Ida. &I.; and, after deducting all on. ' pens., baddebta and directors' let,, and adding the balance of £6,307 es. 5,1. from I cab year, there remained an available balance of £41,180 5e., which it was pron..' to appropriate aa follows r—lnvidend of 253. per share, £15,000 deprecias tion fund, £lO,OOO reserve fund, £10,000; and balance carried forward, 0,180 ss. The first nine months .of the year, the directors say, passed without any improvement in pricee, but after this a Inater demand ensued for the mauu- ' factures, chiefly flora America, and this, coupled with the greatly enhancnd valne of iron ore, has produced the at.ve favourable result. The silver pronete mentioned in the last report has been at wm k during the past ymr, and the glo- ms haa quite emallvd the expectations then formed. The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report and ac- counts, congratulated oh,' meeting on the improvement which had taken place in their work., and their results over the regd. of lag year, and he would say over those of one or two years. The tiret nine months of the past year was clime of great anxiety. MA ho might say despondency. He hoped, however, they had now entered upon a period of prosperity and activity and holesome trade. (Hear, hear.) The importance of their trade. he add, had been brought under their notice by • higher authority than himself— (hear, bear)—aad he hoped and trusted that the chemical trade of the country had before it a prosperous future. (Applause.)—The report and accounts having been adopted, Mr. Ripon and Mr James Kennedy were re-elected directors of the cempany; Messrs. Harnmoti Banner and Soon were re-elected auditor.; and £1,300 were voted to the directors air remuneration for their services during the past year. The thanks of the meeting was awarded to NT. RVNCOIIN Pan...m.llv Drumm. SOCIETY. —The usual weekly sittieg took place on Tuesday evening, in Bethesda Selmolroom. The Speaker took Ids seat at eight o'clock. There was a full house, and a fair number of strangers were present, including several ladies. The Mein. bar for Limerick brought in his motion for an inquiry into the demand of the Irish people for a mstem of self-govern- ment. The hon. member touched on a few points of the political history of Ireland, which 10l to the various agile. lions that have taken place in that land. He then sketched ' out in clear tenor the constitution p erlioevevt for the pin- pow of dealing with Irish internal affairs—each as railways, ' education, manufactures, public works, port officea, &c. Such a parlianunt would do a great deal towards bringing I about the eecurity and happiness of a truly Unitral Kingdom. . The reeolution was riecnuded without a speech by the Mem- tier for Carlisle. The Premier rose to move an amendment ' to the effect that the time for such All inquiry as that pro- posed had not vet arrived, and said that the demand loran Irish Parliament did not come from the majority of the people of Ireland. Ile instanced De two provinces of Ulster and Leneter as being against such a proposal. He also denied that Irish interests were not properly represented ; because there were large constituenc,, in England who re- turned but three members to Parliament, while there were 31 Irish boroughs the agregate population of which antountol to no more than one such constituency. He appealed to the members on the Opposition benches to unite with the ministry in opposing the resolution. The leader of the Opposition in a capital speech said that the Liberal party were the true friends of Iceland; and instanced the naming of the CalholM Emancipation Act, the Act for disattabliehing the Irish Church, and the Irish Land Act in proof. While wishing to do justice to Ireland he could not go so far in the direction of the Home Rule policy as to vote for the motion. The War Minister spoke in aupport of the amendment, and the member for Oxford in favour of the motion. The debate was then adjourned. Notice was gives that questions would be asked at the next sitting, one relating to SOLIIII African affairs, and another on the appointonent of the Hon. IL King Harman to the oilier of Deputy-Lieutenant of County Roscommon. Leave was given to the Home Secretary to bring in a bill to amend the Franchise. The house then mljourned. Cnatton Or AnytrisTranvo Pol Sow me St. tfaraws.— At the Liverpool aeeixes on Monday, Maria Lomax, a respect- ably dressed young woman about thirty years of age (on bail), was charged with having, at Windle, on the 25th cf De- cember last, feloniously administered to one Francis Lomax a quantity of laudanum with intent to kill and murder the aaid Francis Lomax. Mr. Heywood prosecuted, and the prisoner was defended by Dr. Commies —ft appeared that in 1571 the prisoner was married at Bury to • man named Lomax, with whom she lived only three months. Latterly she was liv- Ingat St. Helens with a man named Gray, by whom she bade child, which was about four months old at the date of the alleged offence. On the 23rd of December mere disagree- ment took place between Gray and her, and he ordered her to leave the house. On the morning of the Stub of Decem- ber she purchased three pennyworth of laudanum from a druggist in St. Helens, stating that it was for her mother, who ...materna to take laudanuni. On the same night she called on Gray at his work, and told him she had some- thing which would "side 'the child. He ordered her away, and she then appeared to have gone to the home via neigh- ' bout and mixed two teaspoonfuls of laudanum, which she gave to the child on the morning of Chrialmas Day. On the evening of the same day Me went to the police station at Sr. Ilelms and teld the police that she had given the I child laudanum. The child, however, eventually recovered. —The jury found the prisoner guilty, but strongly recom- mended her to mercv.—Hia lordship deferred sentence.

MAKERFIELD PLOUGHING MATCH. The Makerfield Ploughing Society held their twenty-foarth annual ploughing match on Thursday, in • geld of about BO acres, in Haydock Park, in the occupation of Mr. Halton Wright. The soil was admirably adapted for the purpose. The weather, on the whole, was favourable. Ploughing . . , .•

con cowl a few minutes past nine, and the stipulated ".time Inc work was five hours, being at the rate of a statute area in fourteen houni. The committee draw • hard and fast line, dedding that all cempelitors who failed to complete their task should be disqualified from receiving any prize. Notices were posted on the ground to this effect and a gun fired when the time was up. The entries corn- nand favourably with those of preceding veers and were slightly above the average, numbering 57, no less than 54 competitors putting in an appearance. They were divided amongst the various classes as follows : Double-furrow ploughs, 5 entries, 5 competitors; single- furrow ploughs, le class, 11 entries, 10 competitors; 2nd elms, 32 entries, 31 competitors ; 3rd clam (youths), 8 entries, 7 competitors, and one specLal entry. The quality of the ploughing was described as being goal all round, one good judge remarking that "three was no bad, most of it being good, and all the rest middling," but if there was one class worse than another it was the double-furrow. The work done by the lst dam single-furrow men was described as excellent, the judges having no little difficulty in awarding the prime, the winner's perfornaanm being as nmr perfection as possible. In this class was Abraham Bradbuni, plough- man to Mr. R. Livesey, who has taken so many prizes, but he was net in the bunt, coining in no nearer than tifth, receiving, however, the commenlations of the judges, a position which, however, entitled Lim to the prize presented ! by the Aspull Runt Club for competitors only, whom land lain the hunt district, all the other prize winners coming from other districts. Special mention should also he made of the youths' dam, which was flinch above the usual average. During the day a large number of spectators visited the ground, it being estimated that about 100 were present during the day, although the field being no large the attendance did not appear to be no great. _ The fifth annual meeting of the shareholdere of the Atlas Chemical Company, Limited, was held at the Central Hotel, Widnes, on Tuesday. The chair was occupied by Al fer- mi. Joseph Cook, ea-Mayor of St. Helens, and a large body of shambolders were in attendance. . .
The Securrenv r.d the notice convening the meeting, and the minu. of the previone meeting, which were con- firmed. . . . . .

—The CHAIRMAN read the directors' report and balance- sheet, and reminded the shareholders that the anticipations that had been indulged at the last meeting by himwlf and co-directors bad been fully confirmed by the result of the year's work, lie expressed a confident expectation that the present year would be more prosperous than the last. lie concluded by moving the adoption of the report and accounts as read.
sfl;.rnotion was seconded by Mr. Joww Gnansown, and

,e,.. Mr. Bancuorr moved that the tividend of 12s. per share recommended by the directors be now paid. The directors had not thought it judicious to divide a very large propor- tion of the year's profits amongst the shareholders, but 23,000 had been added to the depreciation account, and a large anutunt of money carried forward to next year, in order to be fortified against any contingencies that might I arse. They were ali aware, too, of the very heavy demands Cl t had been made on the exchequer during the year, in consequence of the extension of the works. In connection with this subject, he would say that, netwithetanding the adverse external criticism to which they had been subjected, it was now apparent that the directors had chosen the ex- actly right moment for erecting new works. They had been able to purchase iron and building materials on singularly advantageous terms, whilst chemical produce of all descriP- Bons was rapidly rising in value and he was, therefore, not surprised to hear the expressions of approval and satisfac- tion that htal fallen Bona the shareholders. On the motion of Mr. CLARKSON seconded by Mr. H. 8188- Nee, the thanks of the meeting were unanimously presented to the directors for their services during the year. The directore retiring by rotation were Mr. I' Bancroft and Mr. Hobert Cook, both of whom were re-elected unanimously, on the motion of Mr. ROBURFON, supported by Mr. B. BROWN. . . . . . . .

Mr. ROB 11:90N observed that with regard to Mr. Bancroft holding .he did such a large amount of the company's shares, hiscoon.l and assistance on the directorate were eminently desirable. With reference to the candidature of Mr. Robert Cook, the managing director, he hardly needed to say anything to recommend it to the meeting. It was sufficient to look at the succew which had attended the opera- tions of the year. If had been pointed out tee strange thing that a body of men unfamiliar with the chemical trade, and the peculiarities of chernical processes, should be atilt to direct the business of a erorkeeuchee that, and carry , it forward ton successful issue, but the mystery bad no en- for those who understood the care and discernment which Mi. Cook handled every question that arose, and there was no doubt that the success of the work was largely due to his exertions.

S;;;;, -.Taylor, and Stead, of Liverpool, were re- appointed auditors to the company. The next meeting was fixed for the 815 February, 1881. Cl the same place; and votes of thanks to the Managing director, chairmao, and offici.ds brought the .proceedings to a close.

YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS, THE THREE PRISONERS SENTENCED TO DEATH. The three prisoners, Hugh Burns, Patrick Kearns, and Mary Ann Tracey, were again placed in the dock yesterday ! morning, indicted fertile murder of Patric Tracey, at Widnes, on the 24th October last. Mr. Heywood, in again addressing the are, mid there was me undisputed fact in the case, and that was that the inm Tracey was unquestionably murderedon that Friday morning —the 211 h October. The first question the jury bad to ask themselves was, who committed that murder ? Was it com- mitted by the inmates of the house, or was it committed by someone without ? With reference to the latter question, as In whether it was committed by mmeone without, they had the statement of the prisoner Tracey. That •tatemmt was adopted by both the other prieoners. Therefore the whole three of them alleged that the house hail been broken into, and that the sum of nioney had been stolen from it, and seeing it was put forward so prominently immedi.aely after the murder by all the prisoners, it must form, as lie appre- hended, one strong no of his learned friend's defence of the prieeners. at his lamed friend endearoured also to eatabliah ancthertheory by which it could be shown that the murder was committed by someone from without, the question, if be apprehended the theory properly, being upou that part of the case where the question was as to the hole in the window of Tracey's bedroom. The jury would remember they IN en.: told by It,. O'Keeffe and be others that in the window of that room, the window which looked ever the foot of the bed, there was a small botch If an inch or an inch, such a hole as might have been produced by a stone being thrown at it. Bat his learned friend night euggeet that perhaps the mutter was committed by a pistol being fired through that hole in the window. Such a theory, Ire thought, need hardly be mentioned. From the position in which Tracey wax lying in the bed. from the position of the wound itself, from the fact that All must have been darkness in the room, if he wan lying in bed in the way described It was impossible that a murder could have been committed in that way. Moreover, the curtain acmes the window would, he apprehended, have sheen some trace of a pistol shot if that had been the case. But there wag no suggestion of any trace of a pistol shot on that curtain From the nature of the pieces of lead which were found M the brain of the deceased man, it wan obvious that a charge of that kind fired at that dietance at the man ivould have spread. It could not possibly have been that those four pieces of lead could have entered his brain if they hot been fired at that distauce from the deceased man Tracey. All the circumetances of the wound were clear to show that the pistol must have been placed very close to the head of Tracey, otherwise if they believed the evidence of the wiedical num such a wound as that could not hive been given. With reference to the other theory that some burglar had broken into the house, and had then gone upstairs and murdered Tracey whilst he was lying in bed, did it not at once strike the jury as extremely unlikely that if a burglar had got into the house, had broken open the box, and hill stolen EIS, he would have then gone upatairs and committed a cold blood and deliberate murder without a motive in Ste world for committing it. They might take into accouet their experience of the affairs of life, but surely it was not their experience in the affairs of life that a burglar, when lie had effected his purpose in stealing, went and committed a ruthless murder. Ile put that must strongly to them, the evidence made it conclu- sive to their minds that no burglary was committed. But that one fact alone, it there was no other evi,lence, 16004 lead them to suppose that the story of the burglary was untrue. But what did they Cod ? After the investigation of the house, after the examination of the windows of the house and the doors of the house was made by the officer and by the doctor, they foetid the windows and every place by which an entry could be effected was in such a condition that it was itnpossible ! that any one could have entered. Fa idence was brought on another point, not that it was adaolutely necessa. v to es- tablish the case for the prosecution, but because it was ' believed &ail-able that the jury should have evidence that would throw light upon the murder, and that avidence was as to the state of the pecuniary means of Tracey and his • wife, the object of it being to show that the money could not ' have been ia their posseesion which was allege 4 to be iu 1' their posses ion, and therefore it could not have Seen stolen, and to show still more conclusively that the tale of the I burglary was untrue. It seemed absurd that a person who had money in her possession should have to borrow. The next part was perhaps the most difficult to deal with. Those ' three persons were the only occupanta of that house on the morning of the murder, and the jury would have to weigh each case as against each prisoner separately. They must not come to the conclusion that the murder was committed and that therefore the prisoners did it, bet they must be satis- fied that the evidence pointed they had acted in consort, and all had the intention that the murder should be committed. The statements made by the prisoners were made ,vith the object to deceive those who were endeavouring to aaceitain why the murder was committed. As to the familiarity existing between Kearns and Mrs. Tracey, could the jury have any deubt that the prisoner Kearos and Mrs. Tracey were on greater terms of familiarity than they ought to have been/ 'Then there were the insurancee ; and as to the policy fed £lO3, the evidence must show the jury that the deceased himself wee not a party to it. He was satisfied with the insurance on his life, and it was certainly improbable that he would allow his wife to effect another assurance. So far, then, as the case went against Mrs. Tracey the motive was perfectly clear. If she killed her husband the money came to her. As against Kearns the eviience was not clear. There was no direct evidence against him but if they coupled the evidence agamst him with the fact that he was on terms of improper intimacy with Site. Tracey, then it was exceedingly probable there might have been an understauding between them that when the deceased man disappeared they would join their fortunes together, and in that way lie would be interested. As to Burns, none of them inotivee could be attributed to him, and if the prisoner Burns took a part in the murder he toast have taken his part as sweet hired assassin. There was no earthly motive that any one could see except that of money. 'They could not suppose he would join in to munh r without mine motive, and the only motive that could be euggested was that he was to receive eome consideration for the share he took in it. That was fair to say on belndf of the prisoner Burns, but then there teas a difficulty on behalf of Burns, and this was the difficulty they had to contend with. Berne woe the man who bought the pistol; he not only bought the pistol but the powder and caps. And when he bought them were the jury not satisfied that it was the prisoner Kearns who was standing at the door, and who went away to ith him as soon an the powder and cape had been purchased? The later statement made by Kearns 'had been moulded to It many of the circumstances of the case. He add Burns shot the man, but how did he know it? The some remark applied to Mrs. Tracey, who said it was Burns or Kearns. Up to that time the statement bad been that it was a burglar. Did not those statements show the jury that the prisoners knew far more about the murder than they cared to tell? If they knew how the murder was commit- ted, and were innocent, how was it they did not coine before Ohs coroner and niagistratea? But up to the last moment every effort was made to screen therm but when the ease was proceeding lot, MI then they made statements showing their knowledge of the murder, and did it not satisfy the jury that they must have been parties to if? But there was one important particular in which Kearns had made a grom misstatement; and he had made that missMtement ap- parently because Mrs. Tracey had stated it before the coroner, and also Meaner be did not know that the prosecution had in their possession floe fact that between half-past nine and a quarter-past ten o'clock the two male prisonera were in a public-house drinking together. The learned counsel con- cluded by saying that he had laid the facta before them, and it was for the jury to form their own opinion, and that they would 110 .0 fairly and carefully Ito bad no doubt. Dr. CORMINS then addreseed the jury for the defence. He said he did not think that it ever fell to his lot to address a jury with a fuller sense of the responsi- bility that weighed upon him. It was not alone that he had to bear the responsibility of standing between three lives and the scaffold—he bad also to bear the responsibility of being able, or, at all events, doing all that was in his power in the direction of unravelling the web of facM, partly facts and partly fancies, that memed to weave around the pri- soners. He assured them that he fully felt the difficulty of , that task, especially when he saw that his learned friend (Mr. Heywood) who, with all his desire, he was sure, to be fair, had fallen into the errors which he very fairly warned them agaiust at the opening of the trial. He told the jury they ought to keep their minds clear, as much as possible, from any of the impressions they might have received from reading articles in the newspapers or from the conversation that this terrible crime inuet have give rise to. Mr. Hey- wood told them also that there were ffiatements from the pri- eoners, and that those statements, 38 matt. of law, were ,entirely valuel.e, except as against the individual prisoner who in mch case [node it. Yet, through the whole course of his case be had so arranged those steementa,—against which he had cautioned the jury not- to take them—in evi- dence ageing the prisonera who did not make them, that he asked the jury to convict on each and every one of then. But that Vilis not all. He had fallen into I another error. He asked the jury to convict only upon indisputable evidence of facts, and ever and over again he had called attention te facts that had never been proved at all. For instance, he had over and over again assumed as an undispul fact that the pistol found seas purchased bv Burn. , he fed said that it was an undisputed fact that , the pistol found was the one with which the murder had been committed. But were these unaisputed facto? He submitted that they were not. All cams of circumstantial evidence were surrounded with difficulty. In the present case this was particularly so. Let them remember this. Had they not seen ceees in which the circumstances seemed most strongly to point to guilt, and yet it was found that the persons charged were pefectly innocent ? Passing on, Dr. Commins said that in cases ef circumstantial effidence mo- tive and power to perform a crime had to be proved, and after that it must be shown that the permn to whom the motive had been traced had the sole power to commit the aft He held that none sf the conditions necesmry to the Coding of a verdist of guilty inn case like this had been fulfilled. The prosecution iM this respect had broken down most egregiously. The only motive was that Bums might have done it as'a hired aseaasin. But etill if they were to suppose that pemons were w icked enough to plan a murder, surely they had so much reason and common mime RA to fool that the fewer who knew of the offence the better. They tumefy had reason and common sense enough to know thet the mom concerned in it the more danger there was of mine one revealing what had been done, and turning upon them. There was no mistake that if either Mrs. Tracey on Emma had any intention to kill Tracey they could have done it it a way not to let Burns know and without exciting the leaffi suspicion. The motive aa regarded Kearns, was a little stronger, although he doubted whether the facts were stronger at all— probably not so strong when they took all tbe circurnatances into mnaideration. Mr. Heywood supposed that a criminal Intimacy existed between Kearns and Mrs. Tracey. That was cruel in the extreme, and unless some evidence stronger than suspicion was given in support of it, it was hard on the part of the prosecution to make such a statement. He had elicited (rota the witnesses that the deceased and his I wife always lived on the hostel terms. and that she was a laving wile. Having disposed of the motive, had they the Opportunity ? There was no doubt about that. That they

were all three in the houne wee never denied for cue I moment. It was the only point in the case. which he I admitted. As to Barnes etatement, he did not admit he was I present in the room ; and did not admit he saw the man who fired the ellot he made no admission whatever of com- plicity in the murder. The footsteps heard by the witnesses were accounted for by Mrs. Tracey in her statement that she went down stairs and then came up again. Dr. Commins next proceeded to argue that it mono perfectly natural proceeding on Mrs. Tracey's part to be taking goods on credit, having two ludgera although she had money in the house. With regard to the insurance on Tracey's life, he contended that looking at the dangerous nature of his employment it was a perfectly natural proceeding. The euggestions that three insurances were effected bfftind hie back were entirely unwarrantable assumptions. The more important part of the case was the circumstantial evidence, and he coMentled that having proved motive and the ability to commit the crime, his friend must also pro, e that no one elee could have committed it. Ile submitted that his trim(' had signally failed to prove that no one else could have done it. Mrs Tracey's statement was not evidence against the other prisoners ; but even if it were, it was not atoll con- clusive. Something had been add about there tying no stains of blood upon the femele prisoner's nightdress, and importance was attached to it at proving that she Won not in bed when the pistol was hrel. But she jumped up im- moliately on hearing the pistol, and thus esnpod any spurt- ing of blood The learned counsel submitted that there wan a possibility of the murder having been effected by wane unknown person—.me trades unionk or member of a secret society—and that it was not the bonnie. of the defence to prove w-ho that per.n might be. Dr. Cummins concluded by saying that after the direction of Ids lordship lie would leave the case in the hands of the jury with the utmost con- fidence, trusting that they would, for the take of jot, deal tenderly with the accused. The Court then adjourned for lunch. The Judge, on the reassembling of the Court, proceeded to sum up the evidence. He raid the jury were engaged in the most important investigation which could be taken inn court of juntice, and in this ease they were not only to try a fellow-creature for his life—they were. ae had freer told them, to try three fellow-creaturrs far murder, because the charge ag.tinst those persons woe that they Mob, and as an united not, and so no to make all guilty perhaps in the first degree. murdered the man Patrick Tracey. The crime of murder in this case need not be deniled by him to the jury with anything like length or precision. Taking away the life of a fellow-crewture, deliberately and with malice aforethought, was murder, and in this case the question for the jury to consider—becaune there wee no queetion that a murder had been committed—Wee by whom the murder had been done. Sometimes the more embarked in investigations at to the cause of death ; whether the murdered man had really been murdered, whether he wasseff-tnurdered, whether he had been killed by accident. Consideration of that kind from time to tinte came before the jury . but in this case none of those features presented themselves. The man had been murdered by sun one, and the only question woo by whom, or rather, the question for the jury Woe, were the prisoner, the per.ne who committed the mur- der ? They had been told, and told to a cettain extent with perfect truth, that they wee, to be satisfied beyond all possi- bility of doubt as to the guilt of the prisoners, and they had been warned, not without ',anon or gond sense, that where the issue was so grave the certainty should be proportionate to t the issue. But he was bound te tell the jury that in point of law there was no distinction in that respect between one issue and another. The person who was indicted for stealing pennyworth of potatoes was entitled to be acquitted unless his guilt was made ont rand 20 person indietod for murder were entitled to nn more. If guilt wee mule °Welty evidence which the law called proper and sufficient, the petty thief t and the atrocious murderer alike ought to be found guilty. With regard to what was meant by the possibility of every convelvable doubt, a bystander who new a crime committed tght possibly be mistaken as to the way in which it was ci mmitted ; and as to the guilt of the pwson who committal it. What was meant was that there should be that strong proba- bility which would justify, in the seri.e affairs of life, a conscientious man acting upon it. Where so much depended upon actual intent, lie was bound to say that the actual ex- ' let enee of actoal intent would never be known for certain by any human being except the motor. It was true that in cir- cumstantial evidence it was always possible that the person against whom it pointed might be innocent ; but where all the circumstances were strop, and numerous and connected, and were met by nothing on the other side, in the ordinary serious affairs of life men were in the habit of acting upon the result ; and the' law told them that if they thought there was reasonable probability brought home to their minds they were justified in acting upon it. The deceased mon wee murdered in his led and undouitedly by a pistol, and the question wan whether that pistol was discharged by someone who came in to do it, or who avaa already inside the house. If, upon examination of the evidence, they found that the only suggeeted means of entering the house was secured, and that it wan in the highest degree itnprobable, if not impossible, that en entrance could have been effected in , that way, then they would come to the conclusion that it was done by someone in the house before it woe shut up. But he did not say probable. It was possible that someone might have been concealed in the house before it t wee shut up; but unless it was drone by notneone concealed in the hone before the house was fierily flint up for the night, the whole rea.nable probabilities of the case were that it was done by someone who was airndy there. Then there was the question se to the window. Did a pereon get through the window ? No noise wan heard. The sugges- tion Wee that a burglar got into the house through a dow; but the window had been carefully examined, not only by what ha might call a professional witnems—a policeman —but it had alen leen examined by an exceedingly intelli- gent witness, who hail given his evidence remarkably well, but who woe anon professional witness. This witness was a highly intelligent man—Dr. O'Keeffe. He had examined the back window sill, and had found that there was dust on It which had not the lent appearance of having been die- turbed. There was a quantity of cobwebs connecting the upper with the lower part of the window framera. Thene were undisturbed. Now, if there were cobwebs extending across this window, Alla the window had been lifted up sufficiently to admit tha pnsage of a human body, the.t cobwebs must have teen broken. Then the articles on the table near the window were undisturbed ; and this could not hare happened if a burglar had pas.d through the window unless, , of course, he had taken the unlikely precaution to replace all the articles that had been dieturbed on the table. tithe house was not entered from without the pereon who corn. milted the murder was within ; and the known inhabitants of the hone:were the murdered man and the prisoners at the bar. None else was knmrn to have been in the houne at the time. The relations between Mrs. Tracey and Kearns neemed to have been a great deal more intimate and affectionate than slmuld have been the nee between a married woman and her lodger. It was roved that the deceased man 'Tracey was insured for the stun of £.34-1 a large sum for atone in his position of life; and what semned to be clear about theme insurances was that at least to the extent if £330 or there:A*oS Mre. Tracey certainly knew, and notably Kearns, too, of the insurances; and the suggeetion was that, knowing of them insurances, there was considerable motive to put an end to the life of the man insured and posaess themselves of the money. That Kearns knew of at least one of Om insurancnu was plain. With re- gard to Burns, he was bound to say that no maggestitin bent taco made of inotive in his case. Ile might or might not have known what Kearns undoubtedly knew about these insurances; but it was safer, in atom of that sort, to say that nothing was proved ogainot h, motlve 'there was no evidence given from which they could tom I title any motive. lie (his lordebip) would not say there watt nothing to nice that sort of doubt against Burns ; but be thought it MIS fairer .d safer to say Hutt Fo far as motive went there was nothing that could be very plausibly ...Led as a nirect motive against the one Burn. What might be found to be one of the most important circum- stances against the prisoner Tracey was that according to the evidence of Cr, O'Keeffe and Margaret Burn no etains of blood were sees on her nightdresa although she stated that she was lying beeide I Tracey when he woe shot. Dr. O'Keefe hadotated that he found a large pool of blood on the bed near the left shoul- der and on the under sheet. lie further said, "I noticed a streak of blood along the sheet. as if it had come from the sudden breaking or bursting of a vein. There would have lat en no streak of blood if the woman and child had been lying alongside the deceased. WelL wan it possible, with this large pool of blood and this streak, that the woman and child were lying in the bed closely packed together ? 11 001 in the bed, where wan the woman ? And why should she say that which was absolutely untrue ? If she were not in' bed, w-hat fact bad she to offer for her absence just at the time that the murder was committed'? If it was done from inside, according to Mrs. Tracey'e aeon., she was in the mom when it wan done. She said she leas lying by his side when it woe done. If they thought she was net lying by his side then she muet knOt• how it was done; and if sha did not know how it was done, thent it was for them to say what was the charac.r of her knowledge, whether she could be convicted of having joined iu a wicked not, or whether there woe any human , likelihood or possibility of hr knowing how the thing was done without being a perfectly. willing consentim; party. So Inc ache knew, there was no evidence at all etf 31Ly violence done in the hone—notl.ing broken, nothing injured at all and there was the clearest evidence given by Dr. O'Keefe that the murderwas thereaultof something sem Home pistol or gun. He now came to the accounts givm by the prisoners ; and he *greed with Dr. Commitne that when three prisonels were charged together ,rith an offance of thin sort, what each one might say .parately was no evideno, against the others. But at w ts a sense in which suck evidence might be material against the person making the statement. Suppos- ing the tin ee prisoners were the only persona who could have done it, and supposing each of them was present and saw the other do it. the fact that he spoke to the other two having done loin his presence, although it was not evidence against them that they did it, was extremely good , evidence that he chose to say he maw another person do it In that dense he did not think that they ought to H.ject that part of the evidence. ,In conclueion his Lordship said he need not tell the jury that if the prisopern had agreed together to murder Patrick Tracey it cue ',holly immaterial who had discharged the , pistol.. One hand only could discharge the pistol, and if hire. Tracey stood by and knew it was going to be done, and if Burn; and Kearns purchased the thing for thie object, to , join in the attack upon the life of tine man, then hire, , Tracey would be equally guilty, and there was no Sistine- lion legal or moral in the CASe. It was one of the naoet tre- , menden issues that ever were preeented to a jury, but I nevertheless their duty was clear and simple. Their duty wete to say whether they were satisfied that those prisoners did that murder. If they were satisfied, it was Uncle duty to eay ton and they had only to do 'their dory, whatever the con.quences. They were not the judges, they were not the controllers of consequences. They most in this case leave them, as they must leave them in all cases, to God ; and he hoped it was not too serious a thing teeny, became he mid it front his heart, that he hoped He to whom all secrets were known would gMde them tot t right determination, and, whatever that determination might be, would give them streegth to not inflexibly upon it. The summing up lasted two hours and fifty mintes. Alive minutes past four the jury retired to consider their verdict, and after en absence of twenty minane returned into court with a verdict of Guilty." The Clerk Assize . I The prisoners were then asked whether they-dad anyth7n., I to say why sentence of death should not be passed upon! I them, when they each replied, No, sir." linen. spoke in a clear. steady voice, but h,ants's voice tremnled very much. and Mrs. Tracey's answer was scarcely audible. , The Judge having assumed the cap. Dr. Commins mid: My Lord, Mary A. Tracey pleads that she is quick with child. His Lordship, speaking with great solemnity to the ' prisoners, said they had been found guilty of taking the lit, oft, fellow-creature, and taldng it cruelly, deliberately, and ruthlesely. A most substantial ten was provided, of which about 270 par- took. The repast era, under the superintendence of Mrs. France, Mrs. Boyden, Mi. Thompson, Mize Rougheedge, and the Mimes Sharpies. _ IRONWORIaIte WAGES. Sir,—Will you permit me, as one of the ironworkers enaployed in Warrington, to call the attention of my follow. workmen to one or two ',narks in the speech of Mr. Capper, which appwred in your Sant Saturday'. home. Ist, le referring to the late arbitration, Mr. Capper nye it would have been unconstitutional for the men to have etruck againet the award of Mr. Chamberlain. I would ask if the statement node by Mr. Copper is true, viz.: Is therm- plover.' statement with regard to the selling price of iron ontrue? How are me to obtain justice if they act as he • constitutionally, when the. just demartila are defeated by bold and distinct false stAnierds of employer. P And of what value is the Board to on under such cirCumstances ? Sad. In referring to the .11lin4 scale, Mr. Capper say, Lem than what is asked by himself and colleactes will not be satisfactory to the inou, as the einployors have to put a muster proposition, or sliding scale, and both have to be submitted to Mr. Chamberlain. It the employers' wale Is adopted, I should like to know what constitutional method wean adopt to obtain what are are told is our jug rights ? Certainly not through the Board. 3ao. Mr. Capper .states the sliding scale principle gives the employers the liberty daring times of depressien, or prosperity, to demand what price they think right without any pressure being brought to bear upoo them IT the men. Wages, he rays, would be regulated naturally, sod much trouble and dispute would be saved I would like to know if, in the past very depremed state of trade, the bunting scale had been in opera- tion, and the employers could hove been sure of reductions in wages, if there would not 114,0 been a danger of the price of iron, and consequently, wages being brought down a deal lower than they were. 400. With regard to Mr. Capper's reply as to uur lam little dispute, I fail to ace why our not paying to the South Staffordshire Board should prevent his giving us advice, for were we members, and our employers refused to he no, and to be governed by the Board, it would he valueless to or, at neither the Board nor its agents could interfere or influence our employer. Another poist in, a large nomber of nly fellow-workmen do not believe that befit!, members of such Board would benefit them, but, on the con- trary, would injure the ironworkers of Lancashire. Warrington, Felousry 10th, 1880. BALLTONGS.

SANITARY ARRANthiMENTS AT WIDNES. bin—flood occasion to go to Liverpool yesterday and arrived at the Midland Foilway Station out in time to he too late. I enquired how long I should have to wait for the next train, and was kindly Informed half an hour. On the platform I recognieed an old friend standing by himself, looking as cross 0 thy two sticks. I advanced to him and asked him how he wan getting along ? Did he live in the tone? He maid henas trying to make a living in the place and had Wilt come houses in it but wanted to sell them. But property had gone to the dogs. "No one will speculate in VI idnes now." "Don't they let?" I asked. No,” he shouted, " how can they, they are at Moss flunk? Ihe Widnes Loral Board have stopped the road to Moe, Bank. In fact what should h toe been the direct route between Widnes and Warrington is now full of pools and mire. It puts wen life in danger to go that way after dark, and you must be young and strong to Lw able to jump Iron atone to etone even in the daytime. The surveyors (and there are four of them) moth have received orders to let that part of the town go to pot I think. The only way to cure it will be to build a public-houne at each end, one by the gasworks and one at the railway crossing." "My dear eir,"l said, "you !Mould not let such trillen put you out of the way. The 13. rd will be buying that bit of land which stops the road up, giving a £l,OOO for it." "No, they won't make it," he said, "if £lO,OOO was offered. They will not even put it in repair, nor make anyone else." After this he proceeded— " Your Widnes Local Board of Health (the name makes me langh), have they done their duty?" pointing with his finger to the mountains of waste behind the Central Hotel. "Did A Board of 11.Ith allow nuch a nuisance an thal to be placed in the very midst of the township ," I said, " Yen :" they did allow it to he put there, and by you asking such • question chow. me von do not understaial thin sort of thing. The Vildnes Local -Hoard of Health think chemical wante one of the bent disinfectante they could have in the town. They permit three feet of waste in Kent.street, Travis-street, .d Midwoo '-street. They In a vrhole cur of houses in Oxford-street be built upon it. People hullo pig-stiee of it, I cover floors of stablen, end the Local Board orange carte to I sprinkle it all over the town Mat before it rains. If they I did not think it W. good for the health of the township they could not do all that." " Stop," said my friend, you are going to sewer the township. Now. I have some expert- ence in these matter% and can tell you thatif chemical wante in placed where you Nov it is there will always be foul matter entering your drains. The WO trorn it never dies. It will enter every man'e,lwelling. Let him trap bin sink bow he may, this awful smell will be present." -Sir," I said, " the Widnes Local 13oard have got a remedy—they aragoing to put ventilating thefts in every yard and at the end 67 every house to send the stench up to the clouds. They say the sewering is to cost £50,000, and some parts will be n large as a railway tunnel. The average price to be £3O per yanl to keep us sweet." He mid, "You have a 4s. rate what will it be then?" I smiled and maid, "The profits on the gas and water they have heen hoarding up a loin; tinie. There in the money, that in owinol for street-miking on West-bank and Fimle Pate-road : and every one who owen money to the Board ie ping to joy them at least when times mend" "Sty dear fellow "lent he looked me in niy face with sadneas), your town, as you call it, could have been made nomething of if properly managed. The situation in excellent hot what with giving £l,OOO for this ; taking corners of roads, poll- inating the fronts of houses at a cost of five times the value of the loud, putting curbs down and taking them up egain keeping a market open and letting the stall. at a price that done not pay for gam, closing, thereby, half the shopn in the town making new roada in one part of the place and shutting others up, I have conie to the conclunion that thin is no place font striving man." The trnin corning up at thin moment, we parted.—Youm, SATUROS. Widnes, Ilth February, 1680.

div.head: GUNPOWDER AND GLORY' vARBITRATION.
div.p: GUNPOWDER AND GLORY' vARBITRATION.

bir,—A remarkable document has lately gone the rowed of the papers. Nothing less than an appeal to the clergy to don abs gay ribbons of the recruiting sergeant. This message of • peace and goodwill to all men states " that a man on hecorn- mg • soldier is entering a most honourable profession." hit, allow me to slate that Mmy opinion the moment a man shoulders the carbine he assumes one of the most degrading poeitions a men can possibly place himself in. Were our working classes to consider a moment, to lust reflect, to what base purposes superior orders may subject them, I think they would prehl the civilians' cloth to the soldiers' gaudy trappings. CerMinly, we hear more every year about the difficulties of the recruiting sergeant, and of the lowering of the standard also of the low Mondani of morality of those • who seek to enlist. Bus still our army swells, and one can Only hope that like the d,g it may shortly burst. Perhaps these may not be patriotic sentiments from a Jingo point of view. Perhaps the bishops who sit in the Home of lords and—with two exceptions—vote for the , upholding of Britinh influenee might moat such opinion's, but still I hold them, and I hope to see the day when on the entrance into a town of the recruiting sergeant he will he mobbed and driven out, not by the meta only, but by the women, who have an immenec interest in this 'mention. Let our English wives and mothers picture to themselves, if they con, the number of bonars that have been desolated during the last few yearn (no need to go a Wag way back) by the war tend. and I think they would sooner no their lads in the coffin than in the arms.. Sir, theae opinions are MOM by noticing in the papers that the whole of the Continent is again ntirring itself tip l that the Feat powers are increaning their armies, that it is just pees I sible we may before long have another horrid Continental war. Of course British interests will have to he looked I alter, while its trade will go to the wall. If the , workingman has a dispute with his employer he is simply a fool if he resists arbitration. Why abould cot a great international court be estab- linhed for reference and decision in the case of disputes be-1 tween various countries' Ruler. and Parliaments may "consider " this question, but it will not he carried into effect until the people themselves, persevering. make it a test question at every elecnon of their parliamentary Tepee.. sentstiven. I think the Liberal candidate for Warrington at the neat election is a humane and sensible man, and will vote for arbitration. The man who now makes a preteoce of representing Warrington, and who only nits for Wilder.. pool XX, might as well Way at Walton for all the good he does in Parliament. AnArbit ration Association ha, been formed in Warrington. Not a church minister would consent to be- come a member, nor yet a Wesleyan minister. Why should not the ministers of all denominations in every town bring the whole of their immense twiner]ce to bear upon this gsettiou of" Gunpowder and Glory " übitration ? Vows,

div.p: BRITISH WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

..... - On Monday evening hut, a meeting in connection with the British IVomsn's Tetnperance League wee held at War- rington, in the Co-operative Hall, under the presidency of Mrs. Lucas (sister to Mr. John Bright). In the afternoon a conference wee called for ladim only, when ailffiesses were delivered by Mre. Lucas and the other Iffilles who had attended am a deputation. and a branch of the association irsui formed for Wmrington, w inc Mrs. Dolde as prmident, Mu. It. Garnett, Nice-president Miss Broadbent, treasurer ; and Miss Amy Burgess, secretary. At the evening nieeting, when lett) seam were admitted, there were very fair atten- dance of the general public. Mrs. Lucas explained the :usociation with which herself and other ladies were connected was the British Women's Temperance Asoviation, which was emablishal about three Years ago. Their head-quartere were in Lundoi., and they had now branches in various parts of the country. Tlity had that afternoon formed a branch of the society in Wei- ringtou, and ahe trusted it would bear good fruit. (Hear, hear.) They advocated total ibstinence, and one reason srhy they were ao ansione to work only amongst women was bemuse it was mid--and with much truth- -that women were becoming too much addicted to drink. There wee a very general impression that it was only aniongst the work- ing chimes they had to work, but that was a mistake. In every does of !society they found that strong drink was a terrible temptation, and, what was more, secret drinking was grmtly on the increase. Dr. Norman Kerr, an authori.y on such titatMrs, had given, in a paper he had written, particulars of numeroua cases he hail met with in which women had indulged in secret drinking. If they did that when open drinking was en common,she did not think that, by facilitating the purchase of Gloms strong drinks by cheapening them, they would be able to stop secret drinking. Secret drinking wan now very common, especially amonget women, and it was for the sake of women that they Iwere there that evening, to urge that something should be done in Warrington to form a society which would induce ladies seriously to consider the question. The speaker then lalluded to the good a branch of their society had done at Southampton, thoogh there were still a number of women 1 there who clung to their gime of beer, although their hus- bands were desirous to give kiln. They liadwnother branch I in a town near London, end in that town the women who euffered moat by drunkenness looked upon it as a nutter of fact that their husbands should get drunk once or twice a week, and that they should have their glass of beer every day. Great efforts bed been made to induce them' women to think differently, and she trusted a change would sant be effeelvd. With regard to the wealthy classes of people, there wan no doub' them wee a great improvement going on amongst them, and they were beginning to see that they must give up entirely there intoxicating liquors, and • very large number of them had been induced to do so. The dowager Countess of Aberdeen, for the sake of setting an r example to others, had given up the small , quantity she Inul been in the habit of taking by the orders of leer doctor for a weak heart. (Applause.) Again, Canon Wilberfotce, than whom there was no more eloquent tem- , perance advomte, bad done everything he could by example 'to lead others to mlopt told abminence principle.. It was a I noble Oct to give up everything they were fond of merely for the sake of setting an example and doing good to others. It wee only by thia kind of ne.rnrpintb.ettterywrrr.rlrlrtee bring about a 'better state of things. As showing the groat increase which bed taken place in female drinking he mid that in Salford the conimitments for this offence hal doubled. In Manchester in 1851 female drinkers were cal- culated al 19 pm cent. of those convicted; in 1976 it liad rice. to 28} per cent. In Swerisea the ferrule drunkenness had inciensed by 200 per cent. since 1951. In Sheffield the proportion had increased from 15 per cent. to St per cent. In Edinburgh them woe an alarming increase ; in Liverpool in one year there were more female than male c.mmitatents for crimes connected with drink, in one prison. She then referred la the rnedical aspect of the queetion, and mid it waa wonderful how the opinions of doctors had changed during the past few yeare. She urged upon all women to abstain from drink, even thoupch it wae ordered by the doc- tor, for she felt eure that doctors were to blame force int- mense deal of drunkenness, and especially for secret drunkennesa. But the doctor. had now turned quite round, end many of them spoke against it. She was afraid that in many instances they had ordered drink through cheer laziness, for it did seem strange that with the knowledge now pomeesed of drugs and chemi- ads, they could not prepare something that would ha ,e the mine effect. That they could lv his was shown by the fact that in many mem where people refused to take drink when !ordered, the doctors generally said they could find men- thing that would do just as well. She hoped the ladle. of Warrington wortld give their assistance, for they had had a most satiefactory conference, and front what ahe bad seen at that conference she wan of opinion that there were a number ' of ladies in Warrington who were very practical and business- ,' like, and she had no doubt they would be able to mrry on the society with spirit, and in that work Ate hoped the gentle- men would help them. (Applame.) Mrs J. C. Homdws (Astley Bridge) urged upon all classes uf wonun to join them in their movetnent, the necessity of which could be seen when she told them that there were al- ways as many people in prieon as them were inhabitants of Warrington, viz., 30,00(). There wee always that camber in prison, but far more than that number 1.189!ti througb,as the population of the gaols was very fluctuating. In 1877 Ithere were 519,0n0 convictions tor critne, and Of the. I /100,000 were for drunkenness. In the workhouses they had 175,000 people, and no less than 800.000 people were in receipt of out-door relief. Of thme 11,800 were able- bodied men and women, and the judgm and magistrates of the land and that ninedenthe of that pauperism was owing Ito drink. It was estimated that the loss of life was from 40,000 to 50,000 yearly by direct excess and 120,000 by !direct and indirect excess, and that 00,000 children under five years of age died from being overlain in bed and from parental carelesenese. Sir William Gull and Sir Henry Thompson told them that even moderate drinking wale bad thing. Sir William Gull, when givingevidence in the House of Lords committee, told the lords that intellectnal workers mum not touch nirnin any form. A etrong healthy carter ought he thought, take • little beer without it doing Lim much harm, but anton using his brain should not Mae dlie at all. In conclusion she urged upon all women to join them, and strive to benefit society generally. (Hear, h ear.) Mrs. Sor-ntwottrit, of Bolton, was the next speaker. and she sand she WWI sure that all present that evening would admit there was much room for earnest work. The sad me- of drink were seen en every band, and every day, and Dave wee no doubt that drunkenness amongst women wae on the increase. In order to check this great social evil it was necemary for all who now indulged in moderation to put it away altogether as an example to others and a way of lead- I ing many out of temptation. (Hear, hear.) She thought that if the women took up this nutter thoroughly in War- rington they would do a great atnount of good. No less than 5.131 women were convict,' of drunkenness in 12 months by the justices of the Westminster House of Correction. What misery must there be in the homes of such wotnen ! The women of the country ought to remember the fact that as they were the mothers no they were the edumtors of the future generation, and as the example set by them to their children wee good or bad, en would their children! ,turn out. It was for the purpose of arousing tetn- perm-, interests in the hearts of the mothers of the country that sheand her colleagues were there that night. She strongly condemned moderation, as moderation was not eafe, and M mothers and Christians they must themselves be eh- melee,. (Hear, hear.) Muleration was not safe the Mete for drink grew upon them, and eery often the brightest and best .1 their dear ones were the first to fall. let all women, and especially all mothers, therefore give up the drink in their homes. (Applaume.) Mrs. Wtrrnmne. of Tyldealey, referred to the great amount of evil caused by drink, and said it was from the ranks of the moderate drinkers that drunkest, came. She dld not sup- pose that any man or woman ever sat dovm with the deter- mination of becoming a drunkard, but all drunkards had luen moderate drinkers in the first inetance, and it therefore became the duty of all moderate drinkers to join the make of the total abstainers. (Hear, hear.) . .

Johns, who was accepted as the "champion " speaker of the party, fully bore out that title' by the eloquent address she delivered.
