THE WIDNES MURDER.

TIIE CONTROL OF NOXIOUS VAPOIJRS. - A meeting of the general purposes committee of the Man- I ehmter City Council was held on Wednesday at the Town Hall the ex-Mayor (Mr. Alderman Grundy) in the chair. The parliamentary sub-committee presented a report, in which they etatei that they had directed their attention to the subject of the emireion of the noxious game and smoke from works of various descriptions. Thee had considered a joint memorial from three associations 'for the control of noxiom vapours—the Manchester, the Liverpool, and the Lanmshire and Cheshire—urging the Corporation to request the Chairman of the Local Government Board. Mr. Sclater- Booth, to reintroduce his Noxious Gases Bill of last year in the present mission. They had also considered the Noxious Gases Bill, 1879, and the provisiome of the l'ablic Health Act, 1875, in relation to nuisances arising from smoke. The stab-committee had received a letter from Mr. Herbert Philips, chairman of the Manchestester Association for the Control of Noxious Vapour, stating that Mr. Sclater-Booth would receive a deputation from the asso- elation on the Noxious Game Bill on Thursday, Feb. 12th. The Sub-committee passed the following resolu- tions :—"That this Sub-committee are of opinion that (without committing the Corporation to the details of any particular measure) further legislation is dmirable with a view to prevent the emission of such moire and noxious . vapours and gum at are not effrctually dealt with by • existing Acts of Parliament.”—" That the Mayor und Alderman Curti, be requested to attend as a deputation on the part of the Corporation ou the occasion of the interview with Mr. Sclater-Booth, MP, President of the Local Government Board, proposed to be held on Thoreday The etrAIRIUNI cold the Parliamenta7 Sub-committee thought that if the Council wishol to make any eommunica. don to the President of the local Government Board on this subject this would be a fitting opportunity for dome so. The Sub-corninittee were of opinion that to a certain modifiesl extent the provisions of the Uovernmett bill might reasonably he supporbd but they did not like to make any representation to the Government without being fortified with the concurrence of the General Pi:rooms Committee. Mr. Alderman Crwrte moved "That the report of the parliamentary sub-committee nnw submitted, and the recom- mendations therein contsinol, be approved and ulopted.” Ile remarked that the committee felt that it would be unwiee to pledge the Corporation to any particular bill until the Council had had an opportunity of discussing it. The corn- seiuo- had not seen the bill wh.ich had been or wan to be pkewl upon the table of the House of Common. by Mr. Pelater-finoth, but they were informed that it was entstan- aiselty list 0.14 Ma Q. Lob :AA session. Acv.rd'-g

to this bill corporationa or other local authoritins would thern.lves hare the power of appointing inapectare of works giving off noxious vapours instmd of their being appointed in la,ndon, which the sub-committto thought would I. a decided improvement. But without committing themselves to any measure they coneidered that further legislation was d.irable, and t bat was the extent of their recommendation. i They did not ..not by further legislation to interfere with ' the trade of the di aaa ict, but they felt that something should be done to protect vegetation. The subject had been before the Council on several O.llAiOOO, and '•he indicated briefly the course of action followed hitherto, which had been gene- rally in the direction it was now proposed to take. Mr. Alderman Banwerr said he had Ide doubts the other day whether it wee d.irable for the Corporation to eend a deputation to assist the members of this fancy association— (no, no)—or whatever elw they might call it. The reason 1 for these doubts was this : We are a commercial community, and we did not want to be parties to doing anything which ' could affect the trade in this dietrict (Hear, hear.) But when he remembered that thin was to hoe general measure, affecting not only thie but all districts—thst it could not drive trade Irmo Bradford (Mancheater) or Newton Heath to Widnes or St. Helens, because the.o places would be under the eante conditions—he came to the wmclnsion that it waa desirable for the Council to afford such support to the ' Government as it was alle in passing a law whiel should recent parties who had works emittiag noxioint vapours oni annoying their neighbours. (Hear, bear.) Ile bed no doubt that when the meseure became law it would be found that a positive benefit had been conferred upon the pro- prietors of these works by their being compelled to utilise gases instead of allowing them to pass into the air. Mr. Alderman Moaner reminded the Council of the des- truction of vegetation in Philips Park owing to noxious vapour., and said it otos the doty of the Council to do all they could at least to minimise the evil. He gave some illustratione of the effect of vapours from chemical works on metal, and said he could not but believe that they were destructive of human life. His experience, especially M his own wmks, taught him that the evil was preventible if manufacturers were preparwl to spend the requisite amount of money ~ at any rate, it coull be very greatly mitigated. The motion was agreed to.

At the Liverpool Assizes Oct Thursday, before Lord Chief Justice Coleridge, Hugh Burns, aged 30, labourer, Patrick Kearns, aged 21, labourer, and Mary Ann Tracey, aged 22, no occupation, were indicted for having at 14 idnes„ on the 24th October, feloniously, w ilf ully, and of their malice afore- thought, killed and murdered one Patrick Tracey. "Ilie prisoners, on being placed in the dock shortly before eleven, preaented an appearance In marked contrast to that they exhibited when they were before the in ig.strates. Thia was more especialty noticeable in the prison tr Borne, echo,l with a beard of a few weeks growth and unkonpt hair. was a most repuleive looking obj,ct. Kearns hah also evidently suffered considerably from his long confinement in gaol, kis face wearing an anxious and weary expression, but in his attire he was more presentable than Burn, as he en beside him. Mrs Tracey had an extremely pole-morn look. All the priminers appeared to feel their awful position, and listened most intently to the evidence tendered against then,. Mrs. Tracey odd Kearns maintained a need, steady I gaze upon the judge and jury, whilst Burn. was very rest- less and seemed unable to fix bia eyea on any object morel than a minute or two. In artewer to the indictment, the prisoners all pleaded in a loud, dear voice, "Not guilty," and during the progress of the trial they were accommodated with wets, of while they availed themselves. Are. Tracey, however, stood 4, at a later stage of the V0C.,11110, and firmly cintching one of the bars, leaned forward slightly, as if she wished to bear what woe being said more tinctly. A large number of persons were in court during the trial, a striking feature being the large number of ladies . .

*Mr. ffeywoonf, with whom were Mr. Mulholland thd Mr. Cooper'', appeared for the prosecution ; ana trr Cemmins, with Mr. Landi (who were instructed by Mr. Husband, at Widnes), defend,' the prisoners. Mr. Heywood, in addressing the jury, esidarthe cue which they had to inoestigate wee one which had excited or much public interest M that part of the county hat it was per- haps almost imp,eible that they could be strangers of the whole of the circumstances. But it nos his duty to caution them to reject from their minds all iropresaions that they might have received, whether favourably or. unfavour- ably, to the priaoners at the bar. It w. their duty to try them solely upon the evidence that would be brought before them, and he was sure they would honestly endeavour to fulfil that duty. There was another matter of ...ion in the interesta of the prisoners at the bar, which be thought it was him duty cm the other side to bring More 11111, thd it was this tbstriti the course of the case they would hod that one of the prisoners, in the absence of the others, had made atatements, and very important statementa, touchihg this case. A statement so made might be, and was cogent evi- dence against the prisoner nuking the staternent,but it was no evidence whatever against thy other prieener, so that if they should find that the evidence went no far as that one should acclue the other of having taken part in the murder, it would be no evidence whatever agaimt the pri- soner charged in that way by the other. Ile thought it right that they should know at the very outset that that was so, so llmt during the course of the case they might not form impressions averse to one prisoner upon the statement made by the other. On the morning of the 241 h October the neighbours wiso lived on each aide of the house cohere the murdered man, Patrick Tracey, lived were arouses' by noises, and one of such neighbours went into the hoe. of Tracey immediarely, awl when she got there the deceased inan,Patrick Tracey, was lying in bed, evidently murdered. Statements were made then—and those, be thought, were substantially adopted by all three prisoners—that a burglary had boon effected in the house, that the sum of £1.5 boa been atoleti, and that the burglar hail apparently then gone up staire and shot Tracey as h., lay in his bed, sleeping by the side of his wife and child. Ou the part of the prosecu- tion it would be his duty to prove to them that that slate. went could not have been true, and the prosecution charged tlmt the murder of Tracey was planned deliberately by the three prisoners, and that they afterwards execatel it, and murdered him. Ile thought it would be more convenimt, pertraps—he should have to return again, later iu his open- ing, to the events of that night—to give the jury in histori- cal order the facts which would he brought before them bearing upon the case. It seemed that the deceits.' roan, Tracey, WaS a labourer working at Itiaprott's work% and that the two prisoners, Kearns and Bums, were at the firer of the minter lodging in his house. The primmer Kearns had been lodging with theta for two years, but Burns had oft, he thought, in the summer of lad year, and had gone away. But Ire returned again three weeks before the murder, and Mrs. Tracey accounted for his return to one of the wit- nesses, who would be called, by saying that he mine to pay her seine money. lie ivent awry again, and he did not appear at the house until the week in which the murder was committed. So for as the evidence went to show, there was not much ground for supposing that there woe disagree- ments betwren Mr. and Mrs. Tracey. There were some statements they wool,' heir in clue cord. which Indic ited plainly that there had been occasionally some little disagree- tnents, thd those disagweemeuts it would be important to show were in reference Co the prisoner Kearns. flat there was no evidence to bring before th j e ury .311 itS WMIld show that they disagree". 11111311 onto lead them to supeosotm that a murder would be .'ommitted in consequence. There would be evidence—and lie (Mr. Heywood) would touch! upon it very lightly indeed then—offered before the jury which would, he thought, show that perhaps the poisoner • Kearns and Mrs. Tracey were .in terms of greater intimacy than ahe ought to have been consistent with loyalty to her husband. However, passing from that, one of the next topics it would be important for the jury to remember was that, in the mouth of October, 1878, an insurance for the aum of Ellni was effect.' on the life of the deceased inan—he was in the Prudential Aesdfance Company—and also that a few months mMr to that an insurance had been effectel in the Accident Company. Of course theprosecution did not allege in any way that those policies were not effected with 051 full concurrence of the deceased man Tracey, fora pro- I posal had to be made, and in consequence he must , have known, and did know, that that assurance had been effected. About the month of March, 187 n, some converse- . tion took idace between the agent for the Prudential Com- pany anti the deceased.mati and his wife,aud they were then apparently under the impression that in case of Tra,y's death the sum payable under the policy would be imme- • diately paid. The agent told them that much would not be the case, but that if they effected a small insurance they would be paid immediately upon dtath, and accordingly • , new policy for the sum of £l4 Ifs. was ..ffected on the life of Tracey. But it was very important to observe that this policy did not become valuable until a fortnight prior to the I murder. The rulee of the insurance association were such that until premiums had been paid fora certain period the policy WAS not valuable: thd it was a fact for the jury 101 observe that the policy di" not become valuable nntil about a fortnight lwfore the murder. So far those assurances were effected beyond doubt with the concurrence of the deceased man Tracey, bat Ile (Mr. Hey- wood) would show the jury that for imam titne before tire ' murder the prisoner (Mrs. Tracey) had been speaking to the I agent of the Wesleyan and ).ieneral Assurance Company I with the object of insuring her busband's lite for • further sum of £lOO. The 'mem, as it watt his duty to do, then en- quired what other insurance there was on Tracey's life, and I he expreased hiS surprise at so large an insurance haviug been effected, and he declined the ...trance. Ile also made nnqrtbrrosos token means of paying the premiums, anti then she staled that Tra.y's earnings were from 25.4. tie 28s. per week. 'that agent would show the jury that the pri- soner referred to that proposal over and over again, lie had to call for premiums upon policies effected in that Associa- tion on the lives of the children, and almost every time he called for some time the female prisoner spoke of this pre- posed assurance. No aasurance W. effected, but the fact was relied upon by the prosecution, as showing the intention to polo large sum open the life of her husband, and the evidence all pointed to show that the husband bad no knowledge of that proposed assurance. The jury had, therefore, as the motive for the murder, as relied upon by the prosecution, the familiarity between Kearns and Mrs. Tracey, and also the fact that this large sum of money would come to the widow on the death of her husuand. With those observations he would pass en to the time when Burns and Kearns were both lodging with the Tracey's in the week prior to the murder. He was not able conipletely to fix whether it was on the Monday or Tuesday in the week of the murder that Burns was first seen there, but unquea- tionably Kearns and Burns were lodging in the house on the Tuesday. Un every day in that week, up to the time of the murder, the evidence would satisfy the jun, he thought, that these two constantly were seen toget her, both in and out of the house. It was an important circunutance in the case that the men were both out of work all that time, and . that even on the day prior to the murder, upon their own' etatementa, they had been out to Warringtth, or to Sankey Bridge% endmvouring to procure work. Mr. Swill, of Sr. Helens, appeared for the Waling!, Mary Jones. a widow, residing at Runcorn, and Mr. Wm. Johnson, 27, Brasennose-street, Manchester. appearel for the defen- dant, l'homas Watson, who ice blacksmith et Hopton, near Wirknworti, Derbyshire. .•

Mr. Swift said the actinn was brought to recover the surn AEI Idr, for board, lodging, and other necessaries! for the maintenance of defendant'a wife, Martha Watson, for la weeke st the rate of 120. per week. undid not think there would In any dispute before 'Haltom:air thatday about the mere facts theca*. It would Le rather a question of law end. question of liability. He wee quite willing that mary fact in the ' carte eliould PIM fully and fairly before his Honour, and that hi. Honour should be placed in the position of giving hie judgment and decision upon the point of law without anything being left behind. The plaintiff was the Mater of defendant's wife. The defendant and hie wife were married in the month of Ocol.er, 1875. The defendant was at that tic.,. widower, and he wee a few yearn—not many, some eight or nine--older than the woman that hs nmrried. They had not bcen married long before the defendant began fo ill-treat her. She [suffered very much from his violence, and she suffer. d to that day from violence WiliCh lie committed upon her within the Met 12 mouth. of their married life. In the month of October, 1876, within a year of their marriage, elie was obliged to summon him before tire justices of the peace at IVorksworth, where they were theta resident, and after hearing her complaint the magistrates bollllll 11i111 over to beep the peace towards her. himself in £2O sod two sureties. in LIO each. Within two or three days eller that, under circumstanc. of great onnpulsion, the wife, feeling that her life was not safe, was induced to sign an agreement winch his friend would put in, and he (Mr. Swift) had no objection that it ehould be put in. l'ho agreement which ithe wife aligned was this : "In consideration of my huelneid, Lomas Watson, of Hopton, in the county of Itchy,l giving p to me certain artieter of furniture which 1 bad when we were married, and also giving to me the sum of £2, 1 hereby underMke and agree to live apart from him, and to maintain myself, and that I will not, nor any pers.'n on my behalf, at any tisne make any claim against the said Thomas Watou on account of my maintenance, or any debts what.ever which may hereafter be contracted by no, or on my behalf." His Head had handed him the receipt which he nisi was received for the £2. The question would be really and substantially whether the signing by the wife of those two documents barred her—deprived her of all claims to maintenance from her husband—and barred any other pereon front recovering an haring supplied uecess.iee to her ; end he, of course, should submit on the tnoet of the prosen- plaintiff, who Co. the Mater of the defendant's wife, and had maintained her for & quarter of the year mentioned in the plaint, that thin agreemeut was no bar whatever. After the husband had ts.en bound over and the agreement gigues!. the wife upon that agreement left the husband, and elm came from Derby to Manchester, and there elm entered into the eervice of a gentleman s family as cook. As long as she was able to perform her service arid to earn her own living • she did ao. But she became invalided and waa obliged to obtain maintetiarree othere lee titan by her own labour, and she went to reside M Manchester with a peron of the name of Davies, a relative of hers, who, after having maintainol , her for mete time, commenced an action in the Maneherger County Court against the husband. There was another action in the County Court in the MOlltil of March, 1879, aud that i action came on to be heard before Mr. Russell, (IC'., the , judge of that court, who, after bearing it, finding that the lumband and wife had separated icy IllUtUld consent, non- suited the ptaiutiff but at all evade, he told the wife that she ought to go back to her husband, and claim to reside with him. In the month of June Davi. went into the court again, when he was assisted by Mr. Coblett„ of Mancheater, bathe judge of the second oc.sion, finding the wife had not adopted his auggestion, and hail net offered or attempted to go and live with her husband, again refused to hear the ease. After that second summous iu the County Court, the wife did go to her husband. The Jadge • When wan that, then ? Mr. Swift 1 rimy tell your Honour it was in the motth of August law. When she went to the husband's house ehe told her hnsbauil that she had come there to reside with hint as hie wife. He had • grown-up daughter and her husband midis* with Lim, and the lambent' told her that she should mot stay there. She expressed her determination to remain with him as hie wife, and he was equally arra in expressing hie determination that she should not, and when she would not go upon being requested, viol .nce was resorted to, and she was turned out of the Immo and thrust into the road. Those were the Inds, and the question before his Honour that day W. whether upon those facts &eel upon the farther fact that the wife had been maintairmal by the plaintiff, theplain- tiff was entitled to recover and he aubmitted as a matter of law—becauee the facts could not and would not be dies puted—that the plaintiff was undoubtedly entitled to recover. Ile could hardly think that before a learned jndge of his Honour's knee ledge and experience it would be necosary to cite any authorities, but he would just cite the general principles horn " Addison on Coutracts" and from "Chitty on Contracts," and then refer to the general principle as further enuticiated and stated in the last de- cso upon the subject. In "Chitty on Contracts," the tenth edition, issued under the editorship of Mr. Rusoll, the County Court judge at Manchester, he found it laid down aa a general principle in these terms Let us now con- sider the hushand's liability of his wife', contracts, made in their separation by mutual consent, or in consequence of the hinhanst's act or misconduct. Where husband and wife live operated it is incumbent on any tradesman with whom elle deals to make inquiries and if he trusts the wife he does so at hie peril. Moreover, if necoories be supplied to a mar- Heti woman during her operation from her husband, mere proof of the fact of separation is uot aufecient to rsnder him liable, but the plaintiff n.ust also prove that the separation occurred under such circumstancee as to give heron implied authority to bind him—that is, he must show that the hua- band put his wife away, or that .he woe justified in leaving him, or that the separation was by mutual minion." That wee preckely the case here. It would be .fficient for him to satisfy any one of been three conditions—either that the husb.ef put hie wife away, .sr that she was juatified in leaving hire, or that the separation was by mutual consent and, in fact, in thie case evem one of those conditions existol, and the authority of the wife to pledge the husband's credit was therefore intact. That was the general principle, es .fated in "Chitty on Contracts," and he was not aware of enything to qualify or to detract froin that authority. Then lie would refer hie Hone,or further to " Addison on Contracts," seventh olition, by Mr. Cave, published in 1375. On pace 135, on the head line of the paragraph, woe this "Liability of the husband for necessaries supplied to the wife during the operation Icy mutual consent." Then the paragraph read thus " The husband is responsible for ne- cessaries furnished to the wife during the continuation of the operation by mutual conaent unless she haa competent provision front Sim, or from funds at her own disposal. If she has such a proviaion it lies with the b busand to show it, and on the creditor to prove Diet it is insufficient. If the wife leaven her home in consequence of n quarrel with the husband, in which they are mutually to bleme, and obtains lodging arid the necessaries of life at the hands of a third party, the hnshand will be rernonsible for the board, lodging, and necesearies provided for her." The only other case with which he considered it neceesary to troulde his Honour Wnn the were laet no., which he could discover, and that was the cane of Eastland againet Birchen. He must confess that at first sight it would seem a if that ease were against him; net, upon the whole, he felt strongly, and he submitted that it was not against him at ell. That caae was yelaatale not much for int particular ease, but for the principle, enun- ciated in it, it being the last decided case and being a con- eldered ease. The considered judgment of the Court war delivered by Mr. Justice Lush, and the general principle, to he derivol from that judgment apporol to be these : "'I he capacity of the wife to contract debts upon the credit of her husband is derived from the authority either expresely or impliedly given by him. If elle leaves Inin without olio, and without hie consent, she carriee ne authority with her to maintain herself at his expense, hut if he wrong- fully compels her to leaveaas bonne he la bound to main- tale her elsewhere anerff he make. no adequate pro- vision for this purpote, elle becomes an agent by neceoity to eupply her wants upon hie credit. At the Liverpool Assiaea,on Saturdey, before Lord Justice Brett, the case was tried of Callan r. Price. It waa an action to recover damages for breach of promise of marriege. the plaintiff being Ellen Callan, a rather good looking oung woman 2C veare of age, whose father is a elogger at Widnes ; and the *defendant, l'eter Price, who was stated to be 28 years of age, is the eon of a widow who keeps a I public.house in the am. town—Mr. Seger was for the , plaintiff, and Mr. James for the defendant. —The I'laintiff stated that in 1878 the defendant's mother kept th, Market Gates Hotel, at Widnes, and she and her sister wereemployed them an servants. She (plaintiff) was courted by the do. fendant, who promistd to marry her. The result of the intimacy was that rho became eariente, and, upon defend- ant's mother ascertaining that, she ordered her to leave. The defendant, ire the presen. of ilk mother, said, "11l thought Ellen would 613 true to me I would marry her, fort do not wish to bring any .poor girl into disgrace." Plaintiff left and ehe had • child, which was still-born. on the sth of Augnet lard. She afterwards met the dotendant in the street, eel sked him what he was going to do. and he replied, "Nothing now." The defoulant's mother had muse to a larger hotel, cool defendant was 11, manager. The defendant's mother oleo owned property in Widnes.—la croas-examination, plaintiff said that her father teed,, claim against the defendant for seduction, hut it had Leen abandoned. She was sure he promised to marry her—The plaintiff's sister and mother having been called en witnessea Mr. Jame. submitted that there was no corroborative evhlenee, as required by the law, of the promise to inarry.—His Lordship said he artist with Mr. James, and directed the jury to find a verdict for the defendant.—Judgment was gioen for the defendant without costs.—Mr. Seger askcd leave to move on the question of corroborative evidence. end remarked that d was very hard upon the poor girl.—His Lordship mid i 0 en. very hard upon the plaintiff, and if the defendant did rot give her eornething he ought to be ashamed of himself. But that waa no businees of hie (his lordship,: there was no corroborative evidence of the prmniae to merry. He could not grant leave to move.

Taking all the circumstances of the case into consideration, lie thought he wa.+l justified in saying that the prisoner only acted in self-defence, and that he did nothing unfair. . The annual sermone on behalf of the Runcorn branch of the Wesleyan Methodist Home Missionary Society were preschegl on Sunday in St. Foul's Wesleyan Chapel, by the Rev. J. Bateman and the Rev. J. Nowell. The annual meet- ing was held in the same place of worship on 'Thursday evening, when there wee a fair attendance. Mr. John Simp- son preeided. The Rev. Untrue Veen/Inree read the report of the parent society, which showed that the total income for the year was £34,544 the. Id., end there had been received £35,590 38.11 d. Though the receipta were no much they had to take into aceount the fact that there was a debt of £7,538 Ils. 3d. in connection with the society. £3,750 had been received towards thie debt from the Thanksgiving Fund, but by reason of the depressed state of trade the debt had only been reduced £1,704 the. (hi. The income for the Runcorn circuit last year had been £56 10e. 104. Only a little over 100 home missionartes were employed by the society and eight dietrict iniesionaries. Fifteen miwOonaries were engaged in promoting the spiritual interests of these in the army and navy who preferred the ministrations of Wesleyan Minifgere. The Cootuenee, who was received with applanse, dwelt upon the eoinewhat etrange fact that so much tome interest seemed to be taken in the work of foreign than of home mis- sions. When he wee young he never inquired that it was necessary to seri missionaries to any of our own countrymen, but as he new older his mind becamediadmeed of this idea. It was eaid that London Wen the greateet heathen city in the world. (Hear, hear.) They might be somewhat so d rprise to three that there were 50 per cent, more known thieves in Lancashire than in London, and this fact nhowed the great need of sending missionaries to thereat home. He felt con- vinced that they ought to fake a greater interest in this work. lie was generally proud of his own circuit, but he mule nay he del not feel proud of it in connection with the home mission work, eapecially when he saw that the St. Helens circuit, upon which they were sometimes inclined to took with a little pity and contempt, raises! twice as much as the Runcorn circuit !

The Rev. It. W.Svann, of Liverpool, delivered a character- I istic sod graphic speech, which was very well received. He [ Worm! to the fact that the society helped over 250 poor circuits which could not get on at all unless they got alittle help from somewhere. The speaker deacribed at some leogth a part of London where he had opportunities of engaging in home missionary work. In doing this he felt the difficulty of his poeition as an official representative of Christianity, which he remembered having epecially pointed out to him one night when he was speaking near to a lamp-post, boo yotingtter saying to him, " Well, governor, how many quid a week do You get for that V" He would advise any of them who emgaried in this work to have an inside pocket made in their tvaistcoats for their scotches, and then they would not lone then,. as two of their Liverpool aldermen had Litely done. (Laughter.) He ' wished the Government of this country instead at tsking so much interon in other people's affairs, would look after their now vineyards which they had not o kept" would carefully examine into the frightful sinks of iniquity which were to be found in our large towns close to magnifi- cent ebops and 'daces of business, and try to improve thi., state of things. In the year 1791, a silver-haired man lay dying in London, concerning whom Smithey said that he paid the greatest amount of turnpike tolls yearly of any man in England, and as he gathered up his feet he said, •• The hest of all is hod is with us." Might tlic benediction of their Methodist Abraham rest upon them still, and might the spirit of their fathers help theni to go on conquering and to conquer. I Loud applause.) The Rev. W. J. EMI ITN, of London, said that when first the work of tonic missions was commenced there were great prejudices against it. So them was at the time of the introduction of gas, which was looked upon with the greatest opposition, and lecturers had to he sent up and down the country to convince the people that OW all gas was not such a dangerous thing, and there was no fay that some morning the island would be blown into the midst of the Atlantic oomn. Ninety-eight per cent. of the working men of London never enterol a place of woe- ' ship, and often looked with contempt upon tne worshipping ; class. The question for each of them to ask was had they ; not been satisfied to go to their chapel, sit in their cushioned pews, sing thdr hosannahs, and receive that consolation which the ministry of the word produced, without consiMr- ing as much as they ought to have done the condition of their brethren and sisters without. Ile was afraid that they had been content to receive the blessing of God into their hearts, and the blessings of Providence into their homes, without duly considering the position of those without. The weaker concluded I.is remarks by a splendid peroration, in which he ref errol to the Yank,ns agencies which were at work on the world, having for their object the advancement of the rate, and showing the infinitely superior platform on which the gospel stood es a regenerating agency. The speech was listened to with rapt attention, and regret that the crowded state of our columns will not permit us to do more justice to it. WUNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. LECTURE BY Mir W. S. CAINE.

On Wednesday evening, Mr. W. S. Caine, of Liverpool (the Liberal candidate for .Scarboroughl, delivered an in- ! teresting lecture, illustrated with large niape, in the Volun- , leer Hall, Widnes, on Om Scientific Frontier." Mr. Holbrook Gaskell presided, and amongst the gentlemen upon the platform were Mews. Eustace Carey, J. C. Mitspratt. J.P., Martin Taylor, P. Ir. Carr, J. F. Allen, J. Heaney, J. Shuttleworth, anal W. Herrington !ones (secretary.) There was a good attendance. The CHAIIIMAN, in opening the proceedings, mid he took the chair with very great pleasure, because be was sure that anything which Mr. Caine addressed to them would be of , advantage to all, especially upon a subject which was of , great importance in the present crisis of national affairs. One would naturally think that many other places bi the world would be more intereeting under ordinary circum- stances to an audience like the one before him than a country so remote, no barbarous, and 60 unconnected with any of them. He could imagine that thooe who were chiefly men of toil, interested both in their own well- being anti in that of their kith Anil kin, would take more intermit in a lecture relating to some of those great countries where our own language was spoken, and where so many of our own people were living and working. He supposed that under ordinary circumstancea they would far rather that their able Mead Mr. Caine should toil them afoot the United States of America, the British Do- minion of Canada' or of New Zealand, South Australia, or other districts where Englishmen, :Amtchmen, and Irish- men were to trc found but Mr. Caine hasl thought that in the present crisis the history and geography of Afghanismn were far more important to them than those places with which they were naturally connected. He quite ageeed with Mr. Caine. (Applause.) The Government, impressed with the dread that the Britiali dominion, of India might he in- vaded by 1133633 through Afghanistan, Imo taken eteps to bring that country into 3 state of dependence upon England and hostility tower& Ruwia. Lord Beaconsfield and his lieutenant (the Marquis of Salisbury), the Secrettn for India, sent instructions to the Governor-General of India re- quiring him to take steps to compel the Ammo of Afghanis- tan to receive* British Envoy at Cobol, and to hold no further diplomatic intercourse with 160,1111, and that was done under a threat of dire conwquences in case of refusal. The then 0 .overnor-General of India declined to take those steps wnich might involve that country and Great Britain in • war with the wild :tribria ;of Afghanistan ; and Lord Northbrook had to returnhooco. The English Government • •" '
India-1

Lytton—who entered Into hostile proceedings towards Afghanietan with a light heart, and at the present time there were three armies, or at leasa three great divisions ed an army, involved amidst the mountaius cud the defiles of that will country. The people were now in a state of anarchy, the Ameer was a prisoner in our hands, debt was being heaped up which India was unable to pay, and which the broad hack of John Bull would, in the end, be called upeti to bear. (Hear, hear.) Now, it was most 'rape-tent that every man in the kingdom should be familiar with the merits of the question --(hear, hear),—because at the ap- proaching election one of the principal counts in the indi.O- ment against the present Government would be its conduct in relation to Afghanistan while searching for a scientific frontier. (Applause.) Thoefore, their friend Mr. Caine had thought 0 right to devote himself to a careful study of the question, and was there to impart the knowledge he had ' acquired to those who were anxious to form a right conclu- sion on the question they would have to decide. The Chair- , man then called upon Mr. Caine to deliver his lecture. and oake,f the audience to yive hi,,. their attention, and at their leisute ponder over his remarks and make up their minds-1 ave or nay—whether they approved of the conduct of the • dovernment in connection with Afghanistan. (Applause.) The .110 was enthusiastically received, said his objmt in addreseing them was to give informatien about , •cauntry which at thepresent time pormiseed intent., interest to the people of England, and further, to make as clear as pos. I eible the history of our dealings with that country, which : had finally brought aS from a policy of cordial friendship and alliance to a policy of mention and annexation. It was much meter to excite intereet ia the election of a select vmtry or the winner of the he. lager than it was to got attention to our relations with the harder countries of India. He was not going to tell them the story of the Afghan war. The Khyber, Kurt.), and Bolan passes, Cobol, Candahar, Herat were household words with them all. 'ffiie great foundation cause of our changed policy towanle Afglmnistan was to be found in that craven fear Russia, which bad dominated and inspired the entire foreign policy of England during the present adininistrstion,and the belief that Russia not only designed the invaeion of India but was able to carry the design into effect. He would say nothing to them about the value to us of our Indian possessions, or of the solemn duty which had devolved upon England in connec- 800 with them—not only that of their wise and just Government, but the further responsibility of being the only civilised power in Asia, with an influence which was felt for good or evil from Smyrna to Japan. If India was threat- ened with invasion from a private foe, we were bound to defend lier frontier to our lad shilling and our last man, hut we were equally bound to inaintain our dignity as th.; greatest power both in Asia and Europe, anti not present our- ' eaters ac shaking in our shoes at the advance of • power • greatly Inferior to ourselves in everything that went to make , up • nation. (Loud applause.) Ramie had a population i of 00,000,000, but it was honey-cornbed with sedition and annulling with rebellion. When she goes to war, backed with I the enthusiastic sympathies of I;er entire eociety, she must put forth her whole strength to defeat Turkey, eyen with the , aid of Roumania, and all the Christian population of the Balkan peninsula. She is without the alliance of any of the great Povrers of Europe, and if France makes some small show of friendship lain only in the hope that Russia may prove the cat's paw by which to gain Alsace and Lorraine. Her navy is no poor that the Turkish fleet kept every Rus- sian war-ship safe in her port. Her finances are Lankrupt, and she cannot borrow money in any capital in Europe, while her funds are at a heavy discount.
